description: Space is hard, Astronauts re humans. We are Team S.M.A.S.H on a mission to keep astronauts health on radar, even when Earth is millions of miles away.
summary:
Six hours of sleep tells only part of a crew member’s story. Satris helps astronauts connect routine sleep observations to a supported next step, then return to assess what changed.

Our working visual tool gathers sleep opportunity, estimated time asleep, current sleepiness and noticed disruptions through simple inputs. It explains the observations together, checks available equipment and medical communication, and links each action to a fresh return assessment. A longer sleep duration cannot automatically dismiss reported sleepiness affecting activities.

NASA research and operational requirements inform the workflow, with supporting clinical guidance and uncertainty kept visible. Fictional mission examples let judges explore different decisions from the same sleep duration, while personal checks start empty.

Satris makes health assessment a continuing task: observe, understand, act and review. Release 0.5.1 passes 98 automated tests. It demonstrates the software workflow; clinical validation and evidence of improved human decisions remain future work.
details:
A small check. A clearer next step.

A crew member records six hours of sleep. That number leaves several questions unanswered. Was enough time available? Did something disturb their rest? Are they struggling to stay awake during activities? What can they realistically do next?

Satris connects those questions in one visual workflow. Our initial implementation focuses on routine sleep assessment, a concern identified in NASA’s Human Research Program. Research aboard the International Space Station also supports considering sleep and neurobehavioral functioning together. These findings inform our scope; they do not establish individual diagnostic thresholds. NASA HRP, Jones et al., 2022.

How the crew member uses Satris

  1. Record the observations. Enter time available for sleep, estimated time asleep, current sleepiness and noticed disruptions. Brief explanations distinguish the questions. Unknown information can remain unknown.
  2. Understand the result. Satris combines the observations using explicit rules and presents an explanation, supporting sources and uncertainty. Sleep duration and current condition retain their own observation times.
  3. Choose a practical next step. The software considers the entered sleep plan, available and permitted accommodations, and medical communication arrangements. Guidance can involve reviewing the sleep window, reviewing a reported disturbance or seeking crew medical support.
  4. Return with fresh information. Record whether the action was attempted, blocked or not tried, separately from whether the person feels better, the same, worse or unsure. Enter new observations rather than carrying earlier answers forward.
  5. Review what changed. Satris links the original assessment, action, return assessment and updated next step. A readable review note preserves that sequence for discussion with medical support.

NASA’s medical operations and sleep accommodation requirements inform the scheduling, communication and resource considerations. NASA’s crew interface requirements inform the treatment of missing, unavailable and stale information. The implementation distinguishes those engineering choices from clinical guidance. Medical Operations, Sleep Accommodation, Crew Interfaces.

One sleep duration, different decisions

The application includes three editable fictional examples, each beginning with six hours of reported sleep.

Situation

Implemented next step

Only six hours were available against an entered eight hour plan

Review the scheduling gap. The entered plan is not treated as a clinical threshold.

Eight hours were available, with reported light disturbance

Review the accommodation after checking equipment and permission. The disturbance is not presented as a proven cause.

Sleepiness is affecting activities

Seek medical review through the available crew support route.

The return journey demonstrates another important distinction: a crew member can report longer sleep and still need medical review because of current daytime sleepiness. Satris preserves that concern. The clinical review principle draws on NHS guidance; adapting the support route to a mission is our engineering decision. NHS daytime sleepiness guidance.

A recorded example of this changing next step appears in our product screenshot.

What makes the approach useful

Satris keeps observations, reasoning, practical constraints and reassessment connected. It also records when an action was blocked, so an unsuccessful attempt does not disappear behind a completed check.

Space station, transit, rover and surface settings provide relevant prompts. Actual resource and communication choices determine what is practical. These are contextual adaptations, not validated clinical models for each environment.

Descriptive charts, text and colour status cues, optional reminders and a small mission companion support the routine. Reminder intervals are selected by the user. Calendar reminders require importing an exported calendar file.

Technology and testing

Satris uses HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Node.js for tests and the static build, GitHub Actions for automated checks and Vercel for hosting. Assessment rules run in the browser. Inputs are entered manually; wearable and camera integration are future work.

Personal and fictional scenario records have separate workspaces. Structured exports retain units, timestamps, provenance and linked assessments. Browser records are not encrypted and can be cleared or evicted.

Release 0.5.1 passes 98 automated tests covering decision rules, observation timing, person and scenario separation, blocked actions, return assessments, alerts, storage and exports. Recorded browser checks covered complete journeys and layouts across device sizes. These results demonstrate tested software behaviour. They do not establish clinical safety, astronaut performance or superiority over existing tools.

Our next step is clinical and human factors review with analog mission teams, followed by a comparison against the same observations and guidance presented as a readable sleep diary. We would measure supported next step selection and consequential errors, alongside completion time. That evidence would guide wearable integration and additional assessment workflows explaining what to measure, why, how and when to repeat it.

Satris currently provides educational decision support for routine sleep checks. It does not diagnose, prescribe treatment, provide a complete emergency procedure or clear a person for a task.
